cards.title: British colonial rule takes hold
cards.description:
The East India Company expands its power through the victories at Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764). In 1765 it gains revenue collection rights in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.
 Personal note
 My grandfather on my mothers side is from Bihar. He chose to immigrate to Saudi Arabia after growing up there, while his brother decided to stay in India. My grandfather only recently decided to relocate to Pakistan to retire, after living in Saudi Arabia for his entire professional career. My father's side is also from Bihar, but his grandfather decided to relocate to Pakistan once the partition was announced.

cards.title: Punjab is annexed
cards.description: The East India Company annexes Punjab after the Second Sikh War, ending the Sikh kingdom’s rule. Punjab is in the northwestern part of the subcontinent. Its western and eastern regions would become parts of Pakistan and India in 1947.

cards.title: Uprising and Crown rule
cards.description: After the 1857 uprising, the British Crown takes control of the Company’s territories in 1858. Direct Crown government is known as the British Raj.

cards.title: Organization and representation
cards.description:
The Indian National Congress is founded in 1885. The All-India Muslim League is then founded in 1906.
Reforms made in 1909 introduce separate Muslim electorates. This means that Muslim voters elect representatives to seats reserved for Muslims.
cards.editorialNote: A dedicated source for the Muslim League’s founding is still needed.

lines.text: Better than the whole world is our Hindustan
We are its nightingales and it is our garden!
Even in poverty our heart dwells in the homeland
Consider us to be there, right where is this our heart
The highest (Himalyan) mountain on earth is the sky’s
neighbour
He is our own sentry, he is our very guardian
Thousands of streams play right in its lap in travel
Live is our garden thereby, the envy of the universe!
O waters of the Ganges!—Do you remember those days?—
When our caravan had alighted on your river banks!
Religion teaches not enmity among people
We are all Hindi, our homeland is Hindustan!
Ancient Lebanon, Egypt and Rome
Are all extinct from the glorious globe
But we remain still in our name and notation!
It is a fact that we have not (yet) perished
Though for centuries has time been our enemy!
Iqbal!  We have no friend on this earth
No one knows our own secret sorrow!

definitions.definition: A name for India used in Urdu and Hindi, borrowed from Persian.

annotations.analysis: “Hindustan” can feel more elegant and poetic here than simply saying “India.” Its Persian ending “-stan” means land, while “Hindu” is historically connected to Sindhu, the name of the Indus River. The name is sometimes explained as “land of the Hindus,” but this older geographic meaning should not be confused with a homeland belonging only to followers of Hinduism. In this poem, the repeated “our” and the later rejection of religious enmity make the homeland a shared place.

source.title: South Asia Multidisciplinary Academic Journal · Historical names for India and their connection to Sindhu
source.note: Supports the shared etymological connection between Hindustan and the Indus River. The comment on elegance is an interpretation of the poem.

annotations.quote: We are its nightingales and it is our garden!
annotations.analysis: A garden is something humans nurture from seed to sprout, and something that lives far beyond the life of one human if maintained properly. The garden metaphor makes the homeland a place the people inhabit and bring to life. Nightingales also suggest song, so you could read the poem itself as one of those voices expressing attachment to the garden. The repeated “our” makes belonging to the garden collective, no matter the differences.

annotations.term: Poverty and attachment to the homeland

segments.quote: Even in poverty our heart dwells in the homeland
Consider us to be there, right where is this our heart

annotations.analysis: People can often leave and uproot their families in search of a better life because of the poverty they live in. One possible reading is that Iqbal presents the people of Hindustan as loving their homeland so much that they would rather stay there in poverty than leave. The repeated “our” makes this attachment collective, rather than just his own. However, “our heart dwells in the homeland” could also suggest that even those who leave remain attached to it. In this reading, the heart stays in Hindustan even when the person is somewhere else.

segments.quote: The highest (Himalyan) mountain on earth is the sky’s
neighbour
He is our own sentry, he is our very guardian
Thousands of streams play right in its lap in travel

annotations.analysis: Iqbal calls the mountain a “sentry” and a “guardian,” which gives it the role of someone watching over the homeland and protecting its people. The mountain is also the “sky’s neighbour,” so its height makes this guardian seem powerful. However, the streams “play” in its “lap,” which gives the mountain a gentler role as well. This image makes the streams seem like children resting or playing close to someone who cares for them. Through personification, the landscape becomes both protective and nurturing. This helps explain why the heart belongs in the homeland in the earlier lines. It is a place where the people can feel protected and cared for.

segments.quote: Religion teaches not enmity among people
We are all Hindi, our homeland is Hindustan!

definitions.definition: A feeling of hatred or strong dislike toward someone.

annotations.analysis: These lines present Muslims and Hindus as people who can live in peace and share a responsibility to protect their homeland. They state the shared identity that the earlier descriptions of the landscape have helped establish. In this context, “Hindi” refers to belonging to Hindustan. The word “we” includes the community being addressed, while “all” brings people of different religions into that shared identity. Iqbal presents religion as compatible with belonging to a common homeland because it does not teach people to hate one another. The repeated “our” makes the homeland something they belong to and care for together.

segments.quote: It is a fact that we have not (yet) perished
Though for centuries has time been our enemy!
Iqbal!  We have no friend on this earth
No one knows our own secret sorrow!

annotations.analysis: The ending changes the tone after the praise of the homeland and its survival. The people have survived for centuries, but calling time their “enemy” suggests that this survival has involved suffering. Naming “Iqbal” creates an address to the poet himself, while “we” and “our” keep the sorrow collective. The poem leaves readers with a people whose pride coexists with feeling unheard by those outside Hindustan. Read after Partition, “not (yet) perished” can also feel like an unintentional foreshadowing of the violence and loss to come. This is a connection readers can make in hindsight, rather than evidence that Iqbal predicted Partition.

wholePoemAnalysis.title: Reading the Poem
wholePoemAnalysis.analysis:
The poem presents Hindustan as a shared homeland through its landscape and the speaker’s repeated use of “our.” Calling the people nightingales and the country their garden makes belonging feel natural and personal. The mountain becomes a guardian, while the streams bring the garden to life. These images connect attachment to the homeland with the places that sustain and protect its people.

Hillier describes the poem as imagining India’s people united across religious differences (167). This becomes explicit in “Religion teaches not enmity among people” and “We are all Hindi.” The collective “we” brings different communities into a common identity. Addressing the Ganges as a witness to the caravan’s arrival also connects that belonging to a remembered relationship between people and place.

However, the ending introduces loneliness beneath the poem’s pride. After celebrating the community’s survival, the speaker closes with a “secret sorrow” that others fail to understand. This makes belonging both a source of strength and an emotional vulnerability. Written in 1904, the poem provides an earlier vision to compare with “Taranah-i-Milli,” which Hillier dates six years later (167). Reading them together raises the question of who belongs to Iqbal’s “we” and how his understanding of homeland changes.

sources.title: H. C. Hillier · Iqbal, Bergson and the Reconstruction of the Divine Nexus in Political Thought
sources.note: Page 167, as cited in the supplied analysis.

lines.text: China and Arabia are ours, Hindustan is ours
We are Muslims, the whole world is ours
The trust of “Tauhid” (Oneness) is in our bosoms
It is not easy to decimate our legacy and heritage
Among the world’s idol-dens, is the first House of God
We are its guardians, it is our gracious guardian
We have grown young in the shadow of swords
The crescent-like dagger is our national symbol
Our call to prayer resounded in the West’s valleys
No one could ever blockade our forward deluge!
O sky!  We cannot be crushed by any evil
You have tried and tested us a hundred times over!:
O garden of Andlusia!  Do you remember those days
When in your boughs and branches nested
our home and hamlet?
O ocean wave of Sicily!  You also deliver to us
Your sea still sings our stories as our story teller!
O Land of Purity!  We sacrificed ourselves for your sanctity!
Our blood still flows through your very veins!
The leader of our (Ummah) carvan is our Mir
Muhammad of Hejaz
The peace of our existence survives by this name!
Iqbal’s anthem is thus his ‘Road’s Call’—“Bang-e-Dara”
Once more departs our carvan towards its destination!

cards.title: World War I
cards.description: Troops from British India serve in several parts of the world, including Europe, the Middle East, and East Africa. Their service in the war is part of the background to the unsettled years that follow under British rule.

cards.title: Iqbal’s Allahabad Address
cards.description: In his presidential address to the Muslim League, Iqbal discusses political organization in Muslim-majority regions of northwestern India.

cards.title: World War II
cards.description: The British viceroy brings India into the war without consulting Indian political leaders. This war overlaps the Lahore Resolution and the Quit India movement.

cards.title: Lahore Resolution
cards.description: The Muslim League calls for independent states in Muslim-majority regions in the northwest and east. Its leaders feared that Muslims would be permanently outvoted in a united India with a Hindu majority. They wanted control over political decisions affecting Muslim religious, cultural, and economic life. The demand for Pakistan grew from this concern about representation and self-government.

cards.title: Quit India
cards.description: Congress calls for an end to British rule. The colonial government suppresses the movement and arrests its leaders.

cards.title: A proposal for a united India
cards.description: The Cabinet Mission proposes a united India whose central government would handle defence, foreign affairs, and communications. Provinces would retain other powers and could form groups to govern some matters together. The League accepts the scheme in June, seeing the groups as a way to protect Muslim political influence. Congress agrees to participate in constitution-making, but the parties do not agree on what accepting the plan requires. Their different readings soon threaten the compromise.

cards.title: Why the united-India talks broke down
cards.description: Congress and the Muslim League disagree over how power would be shared in a united India. Neither trusts the other’s interpretation of the Cabinet Mission plan.

context.title: Could provinces refuse to join a group?
context.text: The League wanted the proposed provincial groups to be formed through majority votes within regional sections. This would give it influence in the northwest and east. Congress argued that each province should be free to decide whether to join. The disagreement mattered especially for Assam and the northwest, where Congress feared losing influence. The British interpretation required initial participation, with a right to leave a group after the new constitution’s first elections.

context.title: Could the compromise be changed later?
context.text: In July, Nehru’s statements that the Constituent Assembly would be free to shape the constitution deepened the League’s fear that Congress could undo the agreed limits on central power. The League withdrew its acceptance at the end of July.

context.title: Who could represent Muslims?
context.text: The interim-government negotiations also stalled over Congress’s right to nominate a Muslim within its own quota. This challenged the League’s claim to speak for Muslims. The parties disputed both the constitution and who would share power while it was written.

context.title: Talks continued, but agreement did not follow
context.text: The League joined the interim government in October, but stayed out of the Constituent Assembly. December talks in London failed to resolve the grouping dispute. Political deadlock continued as communal violence escalated, narrowing the possibility of an agreed united India.

cards.title: Mass killings in Calcutta
cards.description: On August 16, the Muslim League holds Direct Action Day in support of Pakistan. Mass communal violence breaks out in Calcutta, now Kolkata. Hindu and Muslim civilians are killed, and thousands lose their lives over several days. The killings deepen fear during the negotiations over India’s future.

cards.title: Displacement and violence in Punjab
cards.description: Across the Partition period, mass displacement and communal violence transform Punjab. Muslims move toward Pakistan, while Sikhs and Hindus toward India. The span has no single end date, as it's ongoing till today. Amrita Pritam’s lament addresses the Punjabi poet Waris Shah through this shared landscape of loss.

cards.title: Partition plan announced
cards.description: After the failure to agree on a constitution for a united India, the June 3 plan provides a route to separate transfers of power and the division of Punjab and Bengal. The League has stayed out of the Constituent Assembly. The British government says it will not impose that assembly’s constitution on unwilling regions. The plan replaces the attempt to hold India together under the Cabinet Mission scheme.

map.alt: Map of the 1947 Partition showing India, the western and eastern parts of Pakistan, and the divisions of Punjab and Bengal.
map.caption: The 1947 division of British India. Pakistan was formed in two separated regions, to the west and east of India. East Bengal became part of Pakistan and is now Bangladesh. This overview also marks Punjab and Bengal, the two provinces divided by the new borders.
map.note: This is a later explanatory map of the eventual division, not a map issued with the June 3 plan. The final boundary awards were made public on August 17. Some smaller princely states are simplified as parts of India or Pakistan, although their accession was a separate process.
map.credit: Superbenjamin, with subsequent contributions by फ़िलप्रो, RaviC, and Jordi escarre · unchanged Wikimedia Commons SVG

context.title: A rushed transfer of power
context.text: The British government had set June 1948 as the latest date for transferring power. Mountbatten brings the date forward by about ten months to August 15, 1947. Once the June plan is announced, officials have little more than ten weeks to prepare the new states.

context.title: What the shortened timetable meant
context.text: Historians Yasmin Khan and Stanley Wolpert criticize the haste and inadequate preparation. The shortened schedule leaves very little time to arrange protection and relief for mass migration, secure the border regions, and divide the civil service, armed forces, and shared administrative systems. Independence arrives while these arrangements are still being worked out. The lack of preparation leaves civilians more exposed as violence and displacement grow.

cards.title: Radcliffe arrives to draw the borders
cards.description: British lawyer Cyril Radcliffe arrives in India to chair the Punjab and Bengal Boundary Commissions. He has never visited India before and has about five weeks before independence to decide the borders.

context.title: What had already been decided?
context.text: The June 3 plan had provided for the possible division of Punjab and Bengal. The commissions, established on June 30, now had to decide where the dividing lines would run. Radcliffe was deciding provincial borders, not whether Partition itself should happen.

context.title: Who was involved?
context.text: Each commission included four judges, two nominated by Congress and two by the League, with Radcliffe as chairman. The instructions made adjoining areas with Muslim or non-Muslim majorities the starting point, while allowing other considerations. That left room for disagreement over how to weigh population against economic and geographic ties.

cards.title: Hearings and competing claims to the border
cards.description: The commissions hear arguments in Calcutta from July 16–24 and Lahore from July 21–31. The parties submit different proposals for where the borders should run.

context.title: What did the parties argue over?
context.text: In Punjab, lawyers for Congress, the League, and Sikh legislators present their cases. Disputes include Lahore and Amritsar, canal irrigation, and rail and road links. In Bengal, Congress, the Hindu Mahasabha, the New Bengal Association, and the League argue their cases. Calcutta’s port and river connections, district majorities, and the Chittagong Hill Tracts complicate the decision.

context.title: Why did Radcliffe decide the lines?
context.text: Radcliffe does not attend the public hearings. He reads their records and submissions, then discusses the issues with the commissioners. Neither commission reaches agreement on the main disputed boundaries. Radcliffe therefore gives his own decisions. The awards reflect choices among competing claims, rather than a line agreed by all sides.

cards.title: Faiz · Freedom’s Dawn
cards.description: Faiz Ahmad Faiz’s Urdu poem is dated August 1947. The English translation shown here is by V. G. Kiernan.
cards.publication: Included in Dast-e Saba (1952). This identifies a collection appearance and does not establish the poem’s first journal printing.
cards.edition: Poems by Faiz, translated with an introduction and notes by Victor G. Kiernan. London, George Allen and Unwin, 1971. Poem 19, pp. 122–127, including Urdu and English pages.

lines.text: This leprous daybreak, dawn night's fangs have mangled --
This is not that long-looked-for break of day,
Not that clear dawn in quest of which those comrades
Set out, believing that in heaven's wide void
Somewhere must be the stars' last halting-place,
Somewhere the verge of night's slow-washing tide,
Somewhere an anchorage for the ship of heartache.
When we set out, we friends, taking youth's secret
Pathways, how many hands plucked at our sleeves!
From beauty's dwellings and their panting casements
Soft arms invoked us, flesh cried out to us;
But dearer was the lure of dawn's bright cheek,
Closer her shimmering robe of fairy rays;
Light-winged that longing, feather-light that toil.
But now, word goes, the birth of day from darkness
Is finished, wandering feet stand at their goal;
Our leaders' ways are altering, festive looks
Are all the fashion, discontent reproved; --
And yet this physic still on unslaked eye
Or heart fevered by severance works no cure.
Where did that fine breeze, that the wayside lamp
Has not once felt, blow from -- where has it fled?
Night's heaviness is unlessened still, the hour
Of mind and spirit's ransom has not struck;
Let us go on, our goal is not reached yet.

annotations.analysis: One possible interpretation is that dawn represents the hope for a shared future without partition. The image of the night’s fangs makes the darkness seem violent because it has torn and damaged that hope. The use of fangs suggests that something people once hoped for has been hurt by violence and destruction.

definitions.definition: Severely damaged or disfigured, especially by tearing, cutting, or crushing.

segments.quote: This is not that long-looked-for break of day,
Not that clear dawn in quest of which those comrades

annotations.analysis: The repetition of “not” suggests that the approaching dawn is different from the new beginning the comrades had hoped for. They expected a time when they would finally achieve their shared goal. However, this dawn seems to bring uncertainty instead. Mourning, loss, and more suffering may be approaching rather than the future they had imagined.
The stars’ last halting-place gives the travelers a destination on the scale of the bright stars in the sky.

annotations.quote: the verge of night's slow-washing tide
annotations.analysis: This image turns darkness into water. If night is a tide, the travelers can imagine it reaching a shore. The use of “slow-washing” makes the wait feel longer. The washing imagery could also suggest a symbolic baptism. In this reading, the travelers hope to emerge from the darkness and begin a new life. The tide gives them hope for this new beginning, but its slow movement suggests that they still have to wait for it.

annotations.quote: Somewhere an anchorage for the ship of heartache
annotations.term: An anchorage for the ship of heartache
annotations.analysis:
After the stars and the tide, this image brings the search down to a human scale. An anchorage is a place where a ship can stop and rest. Giving heartache a ship makes sorrow feel like something the travelers have been carrying with them. They are looking for a new beginning, but they also want somewhere their grief can finally come to rest.

One important aspect of this line is the final repetition of “Somewhere.” The word begins three lines in a row, which gives the search a steady rhythm. The travelers keep imagining that there must be a place where they can arrive. However, they never name that place. This makes their hope feel uncertain because they are still searching for somewhere to rest.

definitions.definition: A place where a ship can anchor.

annotations.quote: But dearer was the lure of dawn's bright cheek
annotations.analysis:
One important aspect of this line is the word “But,” which changes the direction of the stanza. Before this point, hands pull at the travelers’ sleeves, soft arms call to them, and “flesh cried out.” However, the travelers are more drawn to dawn. Dawn is given a cheek and a robe, which makes it seem like another person they long to reach. They are leaving one kind of closeness because they believe another is more important.

Author of How to Read Literature Like a Professor, Thomas C. Foster, reads a journey as a quest gives us a way to ask what the travelers are really seeking. The words “we friends” make this a shared journey. In the context of August 1947, their longing can be read as hope for the life independence might make possible. The earlier stanza imagines places where they could stop, while this stanza makes their destination seem like someone they want to be close to.

The intimate imagery helps explain how personal this shared hope is. “Panting casements” gives the windows a bodily quality, while “flesh cried out” makes the invitation something the travelers can hear. In Kiernan’s translation, the words “dearer” and “closer” suggest that dawn’s promise feels even more immediate. Looking back at the wounded dawn in the opening, we can see how different it is from the beautiful dawn they once imagined.

source.title: Thomas C. Foster, How to Read Literature Like a Professor
source.note: Foster provides the reading approach. Its application to this poem is the exhibit’s interpretation.

annotations.quote: Light-winged that longing, feather-light that toil.
annotations.analysis:
The repetition of “light” connects the travelers’ longing with the work it takes to keep moving. “Light-winged” and “feather-light” suggest that both their desire and their effort feel easy to carry. One possible interpretation is that the work felt lighter because they believed the dawn they wanted was close.

This gives us a stark contrast with the earlier “ship of heartache.” In that image, grief needs somewhere to stop and rest. Here, the memory of setting out is connected to wings and feathers, which suggest lifting rather than being weighed down by an anchor. This makes the disappointment in the opening more painful because we can see how hopeful the travelers had been.

annotations.quote: But now, word goes, the birth of day from darkness
annotations.analysis: The birth of day brings back the idea that something new is approaching. Birth can symbolize a new beginning and the potential for a life that has not yet been experienced. The movement from darkness into light suggests hope for this new life. However, “word goes” introduces this change as something people are saying has happened, but the author not confirming if it's really felt. This gives us a reason to question whether the hopeful beginning has actually arrived.

annotations.quote: Is finished, wandering feet stand at their goal;
annotations.analysis: The wandering feet suggest how long and tiring the journey has been. The travelers seem like people who have just finished a grueling marathon, desperate to cross the finish line and finally rest. The word “stand” gives us a change from movement to stillness, as though their effort is finally over. Read alongside “word goes” in the previous line, this is the claim that the journey has ended, rather than a guarantee that the travelers have received everything they hoped for.

segments.quote: Our leaders' ways are altering, festive looks
Are all the fashion, discontent reproved; --
And yet this physic still on unslaked eye
Or heart fevered by severance works no cure.
Where did that fine breeze, that the wayside lamp
Has not once felt, blow from -- where has it fled?
Night's heaviness is unlessened still, the hour
Of mind and spirit's ransom has not struck;
Let us go on, our goal is not reached yet.

annotations.analysis:
In Kiernan’s translation, “fashion” makes celebration sound like something people are expected to wear. The word “reproved” suggests that people who express disappointment are criticized for it. This gives us a way to use Foster’s political reading approach. The poem asks who gets to decide what independence means, especially when some people’s experiences do not match the celebrations.

The medical imagery tests this celebration against the pain that remains. The “unslaked eye” can be read as still thirsty for what it hoped to see, while the “heart fevered by severance” is still suffering from separation from a past life. In the context of Partition, this separation can suggest the division of places and communities. Independence is being presented as a new beginning, but this “physic” has not cured what people are still experiencing.

The breeze and the lamp also suggest that the promised change has not reached everyone. The speaker asks where the breeze came from and where it went, while the lamp by the road has never felt it. This connects the image to the road the travelers have been following. They are still looking for signs that something has changed. The return to night’s heaviness suggests that the weight of darkness remains even after dawn has appeared.

source.title: Thomas C. Foster, How to Read Literature Like a Professor
source.note: Foster provides the reading approach. Its application to this poem is the exhibit’s interpretation.

definitions.definition: The process of separating or the state of being separated.

wholePoemAnalysis.title: Reading the Poem
wholePoemAnalysis.claim: The poem suggests that reaching independence does not mean the travelers have reached the future they hoped for. However, its meaning also comes from the language of love and longing that makes this hope feel personal.
wholePoemAnalysis.analysis:
The opening asks whether this is the dawn the travelers had been waiting for. It describes a dawn that has already been wounded, which makes the promised new beginning seem uncertain. The memories of the journey show how much the friends believed in that promise. They imagined a place where their grief could rest, and their hope made even the work of traveling feel light.

A poem’s title can also shape what a reader expects before reading it. One possible connection here is with Dawn, the newspaper founded by Muhammad Ali Jinnah in 1941. For someone familiar with the newspaper, the word in “Freedom’s Dawn” could bring that history to mind. This connection came to mind since I have seen my father reading from Dawn.com for my whole life. If my dad were to approach the poem with that association, he might connect the title to the hope for a new beginning that came with Pakistan’s creation. However, the poem then presents a dawn that has been wounded. This could make the difference between the promise of a new beginning and what people experienced feel more personal. Although “Freedom’s Dawn” is Kiernan’s English translation of an Urdu title, a reader could still make this connection. This is a hypothetical association, rather than evidence that Faiz intended to refer to the newspaper.

Foster’s quest approach gives us a way to connect this journey to the ending. The travelers have reached the moment of independence, but they have learned that it has not brought the rest they imagined. The movement from “Our leaders” to “Let us” suggests that they are no longer just listening to claims that they have arrived. They decide that their goal has not yet been reached. This is the exhibit’s application of Foster’s reading approach.

However, Gopi Chand Narang’s “How not to Read Faiz Ahmad Faiz” gives us a reason to question whether a political explanation is enough. Narang acknowledges Faiz’s political commitments, but argues that a reading can become restrictive when it allows only one political meaning. He asks readers to pay attention to how the language creates meaning, including what is left unsaid (pp. 44–45). Later, he examines the tension between political commitment and the inherited language of love and beauty in Faiz’s poetry (pp. 52–54).

Narang’s main example is “Dast-e Teh-e Sang Amada,” rather than “Freedom’s Dawn.” Applying his argument to this poem is a step taken in this exhibit. One important example is the stanza where hands pull at the travelers’ sleeves and bodies call to them. Dawn then takes on a cheek and a robe of its own. We can connect that dawn to the promise of independence, but calling it only a political symbol would leave out how the stanza makes that promise feel like someone the travelers long to reach. The words “dearer” and “closer” in Kiernan’s translation make their shared hope feel personal.

Narang’s attention to what remains unsaid also gives us another way to look at “Somewhere.” The word begins three lines, but the poem never names the place where the travelers’ grief can rest. We might connect that place to a hoped-for political future. However, the absence of a name keeps that interpretation from becoming the only possible answer. This is our reading of the repeated word, rather than an example Narang discusses himself.

Reading Foster alongside Narang lets us keep the political disappointment in view while also asking how the poem makes us feel it. The wounded dawn, the beautiful cheek, and the ship carrying heartache give that disappointment different forms. The ending responds to the opening’s question through an action. “Let us go on” calls for the travelers to keep moving toward what they still hope to experience, even though the poem has not given that destination a final name.

cards.title: Independence celebrations
cards.description: Independence ceremonies take place in Karachi on August 14 and in New Delhi on August 15. The final borders through Punjab and Bengal are still being kept from the public and will be announced on August 17. Many people in the disputed regions celebrate without knowing officially which country their homes will belong to. Faiz’s poem gives us a way to ask whether these celebrations bring the freedom people had hoped for.

cards.title: Radcliffe boundary awards made public
cards.description: The Radcliffe boundary awards are made public on August 17, two days after the August 15 transfer of power. The borders through Punjab and Bengal have been withheld from the public during the independence ceremonies. Many people in the disputed areas have celebrated without official confirmation of which country their homes will belong to.

map.alt: Map of the 1947 Partition showing India, the western and eastern parts of Pakistan, and the divisions of Punjab and Bengal.
map.caption: The 1947 division of British India. Pakistan was formed in two separated regions, to the west and east of India. East Bengal became part of Pakistan and is now Bangladesh. This overview also marks Punjab and Bengal, the two provinces divided by the new borders.
map.note: This is a later explanatory map of the eventual division, not a map issued with the June 3 plan. The final boundary awards were made public on August 17. Some smaller princely states are simplified as parts of India or Pakistan, although their accession was a separate process.

context.title: Why the delayed announcement mattered
context.text: The Punjab and Bengal awards are dated August 12. Mountbatten delays their publication until after independence. Keeping the final borders secret prolongs rumours, fear, and uncertainty and makes it harder for families to plan and for officials to coordinate protection. When the awards are revealed, people who find themselves on the other side of the new border face sudden decisions about whether and where to flee. Violence and migration have already begun, so the announcement adds to an existing crisis rather than starting it.

context.title: Where the line fell
context.text: Lahore becomes part of Pakistan and Amritsar part of India. Bengal is divided between West Bengal in India and East Bengal in Pakistan, now Bangladesh. The map comparison below shows the division alongside the earlier religious geography.

context.title: What a border could not preserve
context.text: The awards divide connected regions as well as territory. In Punjab, canal systems cross the new border. In Bengal, river and railway connections are interrupted. Radcliffe’s reports acknowledge these disruptions and call for cooperation between the new states. The map below shows the eventual division. Auden’s later poem asks us to consider the person and process behind it.

cards.title: Massacres along the Punjab border
cards.description: Armed groups attack villages, refugee trains, and convoys travelling through Punjab. Hindus and Sikhs face mass attacks in western Punjab, while Muslims face mass attacks in eastern Punjab and adjoining Sikh princely states. Killings, sexual violence, and abductions make both remaining at home and crossing the new border dangerous. Many people flee to escape attacks or the threat of them.

context.title: Protection breaks down
context.text: The Punjab Boundary Force fails to contain the violence and is dissolved on August 31. The armies of the new states take over responsibility. This period connects the line on the map with the dangerous journeys remembered by survivors and in the poems.

background.title: Who was Waris Shah?

image.alt: Painted portrait of Waris Shah, seated and wearing a turban.
image.caption: Waris Shah. Lahore, c. 1859. Unknown artist. Public domain.

background.text: Waris Shah was an eighteenth-century Punjabi Sufi poet best known for Heer, his telling of the tragic love story of Heer and Ranjha. In this poem, Amrita Pritam asks him to speak from his grave and witness Punjab’s suffering during Partition.

lines.text: Today I asked Waris Shah:
Speak from your grave;
Open a new chapter
In the Book of Love.
A daughter of the Punjab once wept;
You wrote her long story for her.
Today millions of daughters weep,
Waris Shah. They're calling you.
O Friend of sorrow,
Look at the Punjab.
The village square heaped with corpses,
The Chenab flooded with blood!
Someone mixed poison
In the five rivers;
Their flow
Watered the Punjab.
Poison has sprouted
From this fertile land.
Look, how far the red has spread.
Curse how far the red has spread!
Poisoned air
Floated into the jungles
Turning all bamboo flutes
To snakes
Biting everyone's lips;
Their tongue tips rose up
And quickly all parts
Of the Punjab turned blue.
Song is crushed in every throat;
Every spinning wheel's thread is snapped;
Friends parted from one another;
The hum of spinning wheels fell silent.
Oars have left all boats
And float in the current;
Peepal branches with swings
Lie broken.
Where is the grove where love songs
Used to echo, where the flute?
All Ranjha's brothers
Have forgotten how to play the flute.
Blood keeps falling upon the earth,
Oozing out drop by drop from graves.
The queens of love
Weep in tombs.
It seems all people have become Kaidos,
Thieves of beauty and love--
Where should I search out
Another Waris Shah.
Waris Shah!
Open your grave;
Write a new page
In the Book of Love.

segments.quote: Today I asked Waris Shah:
Speak from your grave;
Open a new chapter
In the Book of Love.

annotations.analysis: Why does the speaker call on someone who has died, specifically a poet? Asking him to write again suggests that the current suffering of the people demands another story.

cards.title: Auden · Partition
cards.description: W. H. Auden looks back at how the border was drawn. Although the poem describes the events of 1947, it was written years later. This gives us a way to look at how Partition is remembered after it happens.
cards.composition: Written by December 1966, when an earlier version appeared in The Atlantic.
cards.publication: The Atlantic, December 1966. The archive preserves an earlier version with wording that differs from the text displayed here. The original magazine page number has not been verified. City Without Walls, Faber, 1969. The Auden Society lists the Random House edition in 1970.
cards.edition: Collected Poems, edited by Edward Mendelson. Modern Library, 2007, pp. 802–803. This is the edition identified in the exhibit brief.

lines.text: Unbiased at least he was when he arrived on his mission,
Having never set eyes on the land he was called to partition
Between two peoples fanatically at odds,
With their different diets and incompatible gods.
"Time," they had briefed him in London, "is short. It's too late
For mutual reconciliation or rational debate:
The only solution now lies in separation.
The Viceroy thinks, as you will see from his letter,
That the less you are seen in his company the better,
So we've arranged to provide you with other accommodation.
We can give you four judges, two Moslem and two Hindu,
To consult with, but the final decision must rest with you."
Shut up in a lonely mansion, with police night and day
Patrolling the gardens to keep the assassins away,
He got down to work, to the task of settling the fate
Of millions. The maps at his disposal were out of date
And the Census Returns almost certainly incorrect,
But there was no time to check them, no time to inspect
Contested areas. The weather was frightfully hot,
And a bout of dysentery kept him constantly on the trot,
But in seven weeks it was done, the frontiers decided,
A continent for better or worse divided.
The next day he sailed for England, where he could quickly forget
The case, as a good lawyer must. Return he would not,
Afraid, as he told his Club, that he might get shot.

cards.title: Bangladesh’s War of Liberation and independence
cards.description: The eastern part of Pakistan, formed from East Bengal in the 1947 Partition and later known as East Pakistan, becomes Bangladesh in 1971. Following the Pakistani army’s crackdown on March 25, Bengali nationalists declare independence on March 26. The War of Liberation that follows brings mass violence and displacement, with millions seeking refuge in India. India intervenes militarily in December. Pakistani forces surrender in Dhaka on December 16. March 26 marks the declaration of independence, while December 16 marks the end of the war.

lines.text: Kites hover over corpses in your city
In much the same way they do
In my city, on its crossroads,
When bodies fall
Prey to police firing
The vultures begin to descend
In this, our two countries
So much is common among the common people.

poets.name: Muhammad Iqbal
poets.description: His poems give us a way to ask what home meant before Partition. “Taranah-i-Hindi” imagines India as a shared homeland, while “Taranah-i-Milli” imagines a Muslim community that crosses borders.

paragraphs: Muhammad Iqbal was born in Sialkot in 1877 and was educated in Sialkot and Lahore. He later studied at Cambridge and earned a doctorate in Munich. He returned to Lahore to practise law and develop his work as a poet and thinker.
His early education and writing connected him with Urdu and Persian literary traditions. The questions about home and community in his poems came from this world before the division of British India.

Iqbal died in Lahore on April 21, 1938, nine years before Partition. His card therefore focuses on upbringing and intellectual background rather than showing a 1947 migration that he could not have made.

poets.name: Faiz Ahmad Faiz
poets.description: His Urdu poem “Freedom’s Dawn” looks at independence through a dawn that falls short of what people hoped for.

paragraphs: Faiz grew up in the Sialkot region of Punjab. His schooling included Urdu, Persian, and Arabic. He later studied English and Arabic at colleges in Lahore.
He began teaching at M.A.O. College in Amritsar in 1935 and later taught at Hailey College in Lahore. His work moved between poetry, education, and journalism.

Baran Farooqi’s introduction places him at the Pakistan Times in Lahore in early 1947. The map distinguishes these documented places from a refugee journey. It does not claim that his move to Lahore was caused by the August division.

poets.name: Amrita Pritam
poets.description: Her Punjabi poem “To Waris Shah” calls on an earlier Punjabi poet to witness the suffering of a divided Punjab. Waris Shah wrote Heer, a Punjabi love story set in the same region.

paragraphs: Amrita Pritam was born in Gujranwala in 1919, in what is now Pakistan. She began writing in Punjabi and later also wrote in Hindi. She worked in poetry and fiction, and moved to Delhi following Partition.

Her place in this exhibit comes from “To Waris Shah,” which addresses the suffering of Punjab through an earlier Punjabi poet. Her own move across the new border makes Partition part of her life as well as a subject of her writing.

poets.name: Gulzar
poets.description: His writing looks back on childhood displacement and explores how the border continues to shape memory. “Karachi” comes from the collection Footprints on Zero Line.

paragraphs: Gulzar was born as Sampuran Singh Kalra in Dina. In his interview with Asif Noorani, he recalls writing Urdu there and moving to Delhi shortly before Partition. His early move should not be dated as a flight after the August border announcement.

In his Youthink interview, he describes his father bringing relatives and people from their village into the family’s Delhi home during Partition. He later moved to Bombay, where his elder brother helped support part of the family. He also describes interrupted studies and work in a motor garage.
These accounts connect his writing to the loss of a childhood home and the pressure of rebuilding family life. The map shows those places without filling in an unverified route between them.

poets.name: W. H. Auden
poets.description: His poem “Partition” looks back at the drawing of the border through Cyril Radcliffe, the British official who chaired the boundary commissions.

paragraphs: Wystan Hugh Auden was born in York in 1907 and grew up in Birmingham. At Oxford, his interest in poetry developed alongside friendships with Stephen Spender and Christopher Isherwood.

He travelled beyond Britain and moved to the United States in 1939. That move was separate from the 1947 Partition of British India. His place in this exhibit is as a poet looking back at the border’s creation, rather than as someone displaced across it.

His upbringing and education help place his later writing in a different context from Pritam’s and Gulzar’s accounts of losing a home. The contrast lets readers consider who is speaking about Partition and how close they were to its effects.

partitionContext.text: Auden’s move to the United States was in 1939. The biography does not place him on a 1947 Partition migration route.

photographs.title: Leaving with what could be carried
photographs.date: Scene identified as 1947 · archive record dated February 1954
photographs.caption: The Government of India’s photo record identifies this as a convoy of evacuees travelling from West Pakistan to India in 1947. The catalogue entry is dated February 1954, so the scene date and record date are kept separate.
photographs.alt: A group of evacuees with vehicles, carts, belongings, and a camel in an open landscape.
photographs.rights: Public domain, as recorded by Wikimedia Commons

story.title: Journeys on foot and by vehicle
story.text: BFI’s archival film of arrivals in Lahore shows people travelling with different resources. Some brought cars and belongings, while others made the journey on foot. The footage offers another view of the movement that a single photograph can only partly show.

photographs.title: Finding space on a train
photographs.date: Partition-era scene · archive record dated February 1954
photographs.caption: At Ambala station, travellers sit on carriage roofs as people stand beside the train. The government record calls it a refugee special and describes the carriages as full. Its catalogue entry is dated February 1954.
photographs.alt: Travellers and bundles crowd the roofs of railway carriages at Ambala while people stand beside the tracks.
photographs.rights: Public domain, as recorded by Wikimedia Commons

story.title: Twelve days by rail, then three days at sea
story.text: In an interview summary shared by The 1947 Partition Archive, Saleem Murtaza Qureshi remembers leaving Shimla with his family. They had hoped to reach Lahore directly. Instead, their journey took them through Kalka to Bombay over twelve days. After staying at a military camp, they boarded a ship for Karachi. He recalls three more days at sea and seasickness on the crossing.
story.sourceTitle: Saleem Murtaza Qureshi · interview summary, The 1947 Partition Archive, reproduced in The News (2016)

photographs.title: From Delhi station to a camp
photographs.caption: The original government caption identifies these people as refugees being taken from Delhi Railway Station to camps. Reaching a station was one part of the journey. Transport and a place to stay still had to be found.
photographs.alt: Adults and children gather beside an open vehicle carrying refugees from Delhi Railway Station toward camps.
photographs.rights: Public domain, as recorded by Wikimedia Commons

story.title: Arriving did not always mean having a home
story.text: A September 1947 report reproduced by The National Archives records refugees in Delhi staying with friends and relatives as well as in camps. Another official report describes movement by refugee trains and motor lorries. These records show how travel continued through stations, temporary accommodation, and organised transport.
story.sourceTitle: The National Archives · Indian independence, part two, official reports on refugees

photographs.title: A crowd in Karachi
photographs.caption: Crowds surround a carriage during the Mountbattens’ visit to Karachi at the transfer of power. The photograph records a public occasion in the city. The separate account below recalls arriving there by sea.
photographs.alt: A large crowd surrounds a horse-drawn carriage during the Mountbattens’ visit to Karachi in August 1947.
photographs.credit: Photographer unidentified · reproduced by BBC Urdu, via Wikimedia Commons
photographs.rights: Public domain, as recorded by Wikimedia Commons

story.title: Reaching Karachi by ship
story.text: In a recorded account shared by the Citizens Archive of Pakistan, Sugrah Kazmi remembers finding space aboard the Dumra in the ship’s basement. After reaching Karachi, her family stayed with relatives. She also recalls luggage being lost along the way. Her account gives a sense of arrival as the beginning of another period of uncertainty.
story.sourceTitle: Sugrah Kazmi · Citizens Archive of Pakistan interview, shared by Dawn Images (2018)

photographs.title: Fear and uncertainty in Punjab
photographs.caption: A refugee camp in Punjab during Partition. It gives a view of the insecurity and displacement of this period. It does not show Shergarh or the people described in the passage below.
photographs.alt: People walk between rows of tents in a refugee camp in Punjab.
photographs.rights: Public domain in India, as recorded by Wikimedia Commons

quotation.text: Nonetheless, three months of pure terror followed. “I have never known a period of greater fear and uncertainty,” he says. Shergarh was surrounded by Sikh villages. Once killings began, the villagers braced themselves for an attack every day. “Wild bands of marauding men armed with sickles, axes and swords roamed the open countryside, killing and mutilating anyone they found of the opposite faith.”
quotation.attribution: Moni Mohsin, recounting her father Syed Mohammed Mohsin’s memories of Shergarh · The Guardian (2017)

story.title: Remaining at home did not mean being safe
story.text: Syed Mohammed Mohsin’s village became part of Pakistan, and he did not have to leave his ancestral home. His recollection shows that even those who stayed could live in fear of an attack. This account describes one Muslim family’s experience in Punjab, and similar violence occured to Hindus and Sikhs in other villages.
story.sourceTitle: Read Moni Mohsin’s account in The Guardian

partition.title: Religious communities before Partition and the new borders
partition.intro: Compare where religious communities lived before Partition with the countries created in 1947. Start with Punjab’s district majorities, look at the wider subcontinent, then switch to the borders. The maps use different scales and dates.
partition.reading: A majority colour does not mean everyone in an area shared that religion. Hindus and Sikhs lived in western Punjab, and Muslims lived in eastern Punjab. When the border divided the province, many fled across it in opposite directions. Others stayed. Religion and location alone cannot tell us whether a particular person moved.
partition.example: For example, Amrita Pritam left Lahore for India, while Syed Mohammed Mohsin remained in Shergarh, which became part of Pakistan. His account below shows that staying at home could still mean living in fear.

views.label: Punjab majorities · 1941
views.alt: Map of pre-Partition Punjab districts, with Muslim-majority districts in green, non-Muslim-majority districts in pink, and princely states in yellow.
views.caption: Punjab before Partition. Green marks Muslim-majority districts and pink marks non-Muslim-majority districts. Yellow identifies princely states, not a religion. This map groups Hindus, Sikhs, and other non-Muslims together and does not show population percentages.
views.note: The Commons record describes this later map as based on the 1941 census. It shows district majorities, not the 1947 border or individual villages. Gurdaspur illustrates why a majority map cannot substitute for the boundary award, since the district itself was divided.
views.credit: Khan Ahmed Raza · unchanged map from Wikimedia Commons (2015)

views.label: Wider religious pattern · 1909
views.alt: 1909 map of prevailing religions across British India, with Hindu regions in pink, Muslim regions in green, and Sikh areas marked with diagonal lines in Punjab.
views.caption: The wider pre-Partition pattern. Pink marks Hindu areas, green Muslim areas, and diagonal shading Sikh areas. Yellow marks Buddhist areas, blue Christian areas, and purple areas described by the colonial map as “Animist.”
views.note: Published in 1909 using the 1901 census. This is an earlier overview, not a census map of 1947 or a complete picture of religious diversity within each area. The original colonial labels are preserved.
views.credit: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Oxford University Press (1909) · cropped scan via Fowler&fowler and Wikimedia Commons

views.alt: Map of the 1947 Partition showing India, the western and eastern parts of Pakistan, and the divisions of Punjab and Bengal.
views.caption: The 1947 division of British India. Pakistan was formed in two separated regions, to the west and east of India. East Bengal became part of Pakistan and is now Bangladesh. This overview also marks Punjab and Bengal, the two provinces divided by the new borders.
views.note: This is a later explanatory map of the eventual division, not a map issued with the June 3 plan. The final boundary awards were made public on August 17. Some smaller princely states are simplified as parts of India or Pakistan, although their accession was a separate process.
views.credit: Superbenjamin, with subsequent contributions by फ़िलप्रो, RaviC, and Jordi escarre · unchanged Wikimedia Commons SVG
views.label: Partition borders · 1947

partition.standaloneIntro: These three maps follow religious communities before Partition and the borders created during it. The Punjab view shows district majorities in 1941, the wider overview was published in 1909, and the final map shows the 1947 division. They are not a before-and-after census comparison. Select any map to read it at full size.
